title: Ergodic Risk Measures: Towards a Risk-Aware Foundation for Continual Reinforcement Learning
claim: The standard agent-environment interaction loop is extended with a risk-attitude component that makes observations risk-aware.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, shared loop shape with added pink barrier
description: Two side-by-side panels, labeled a) and b), each showing an agent-environment interaction loop. In panel a), a blue robot dog icon (Agent) on the left and a globe icon (Environment) on the right are joined by two arrows. The top arrow carries action A_t from agent to environment, and the bottom arrow carries observation O_t back. Panel b) has the same layout in magenta/maroon. The robot is now labeled 'Risk-Aware Agent'. A pink translucent slab labeled 'Risk Attitude' sits on the return path. The observation O_t passes through it and comes out as the augmented observation Õ_t = (O_t, τ_t) in magenta. The new magenta element draws the eye first, and the shared structure makes the difference obvious.
caption: A comparison of: a) the continual RL framework proposed in [ref], and b) the risk-aware generalization of the framework proposed in this work.
abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (continual RL) seeks to formalize the notions of lifelong learning and endless adaptation in RL. In particular, the aim of continual RL is to develop RL agents that can maintain a careful balance between retaining useful information and adapting to new situations. To date, continual RL has been explored almost exclusively through the lens of risk-neutral decision-making, in which the agent aims to optimize the expected long-run performance. In this work, we present the first formal theoretical treatment of continual RL through the lens of risk-aware decision-making, in which the behaviour of the agent is directed towards optimizing a measure of long-run performance beyond the mean. In particular, we show that the classical theory of risk measures, widely used as a theoretical foundation in non-continual risk-aware RL, is, in its current form, incompatible with continual learning. Then, building on this insight, we extend risk measure theory into the continual setting by introducing a new class of ergodic risk measures, and showing that it is compatible with continual learning. Finally, we provide a case study of continual risk-aware learning, along with empirical results, which show the intuitive appeal of ergodic risk measures in continual settings.
